<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Limb Isolation?

**Limb isolation separates an arm or leg from the torso, other limbs, or mat supports that help the opponent move and defend it.**

Control the shoulder or hip as well as the wrist or ankle. Place a barrier on the return route before changing grips or advancing position.

</section>

<section id="building-blocks" class="content-section">

## Building Blocks
- Identify which contacts support the target limb.
- Control the shoulder or hip as well as the endpoint.
- Place a knee, shin, or other barrier on the reconnection route.
- Keep your own base while moving closer to the isolated limb.


</section>

<section id="prerequisites" class="content-section">

## Prerequisites
**Support inventory**: Read what feeds the target limb its strength: connection to the torso, help from the opposite arm or leg, a post on the mat, and the orientation of the hips behind it.

**Proximal joint control**: Manage the shoulder or the hip so that endpoint control cannot simply be rotated away, treating a wrist or ankle grip as a handle rather than as the isolation itself.

**Barrier construction**: Place a knee, shin, shoulder or head across the reconnection line so the elbow or knee cannot travel home without first moving your whole structure.

**Grip stripping and extraction**: Break the opponent's defensive grips — hand clasp, gable grip, lapel or belt anchor — in the order that costs them the most support, then extract with the hips rather than the arms.

**Body-behind-the-limb positioning**: Move your hips and chest to the isolated side instead of pulling the limb toward you, so structure rather than arm strength holds the separation open.

**Reconnection defense**: Return an isolated elbow to the ribs or knee to the chest, re-orient the joint out of the attacker's lever line, and rebuild a post before ever attempting to withdraw the limb.

**Release judgment**: Recognize when the barrier has failed and the isolation is gone, and give the limb back early to keep position instead of chasing a finish into a scramble.



</section>

<section id="where-to-apply" class="content-section">

## Where to Apply
**High Mount**: Keep an elbow separated from the ribs to remove a defensive frame and prepare an armbar entry.

**Butterfly Guard**: Use an overhook or arm drag to occupy the hand that would post on the sweep side.

**Headquarters Position**: Contain one leg between your own so the guard player cannot easily bring both knees back in front.

**Back Control**: Trap one arm while maintaining chest contact to reduce the hands available for defensive grip fighting.



</section>

<section id="how-to-apply" class="content-section">

## How to Apply
1. **Do I need a limb at all, or only position?**: Decide whether isolating buys a pass, a sweep or a finish; if the position is available without it, take the position and leave the limb alone.
2. **Which limb is already least supported?**: Target what the opponent has already committed — a reaching arm, a posted leg, an over-extended knee — rather than manufacturing a target from a neutral frame.
3. **What is feeding that limb strength?**: Name the supports explicitly: torso connection, the opposite limb, a mat post, hip orientation. Remove them in the order that costs the opponent the most.
4. **Can I reach the proximal joint?**: Establish shoulder or hip control first. If only the wrist or ankle is available, treat it as a handle to travel along, not as the isolation.
5. **Where is the reconnection route?**: Build a barrier — knee, shin, shoulder or head — across the return path before advancing the attack by a single inch.
6. **Is my base still intact?**: Check your own posts and hip line. If separating the limb costs you base, move your body closer to the target instead of pulling harder on it.
7. **Has the isolation already failed?**: If the elbow reaches the ribs or the knees rejoin, release, re-take position, and re-enter rather than forcing a finish through a rebuilt structure.
8. **Am I the one being isolated?**: Reconnect and re-orient before attempting withdrawal, and tap early if the joint is already loaded — pulling out of a good line finishes the attack for them.


</section>

<section id="mistakes-to-avoid" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## Mistakes to Avoid
- **Mistake**: Holding only the wrist or ankle
  - **Consequence**: The opponent turns the shoulder or hip and reconnects the limb.
  - **Correction**: Control above the joint and use the endpoint as a handle.
- **Mistake**: Separating without blocking the return
  - **Consequence**: The limb reconnects as soon as you change grips or position.
  - **Correction**: Place a structural barrier on the return route before moving on.
- **Mistake**: Reaching away from your base
  - **Consequence**: The opponent uses the gap to reverse or move into your space.
  - **Correction**: Bring your hips and chest toward the isolated side instead of extending your arms farther.


</section>

<section id="how-to-practice" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Practice
**Elbow reconnection** (Focus: Block the return route with body position.)
Start in a light top pin. One partner separates an elbow from the ribs while the other gently reconnects it; no submission grips. Reset on separation or reconnection and switch roles.

**Single-leg passing control** (Focus: Apply isolation to passing.)
Start in Headquarters Position. The passer contains one leg while the guard player slowly brings both knees back in front. Reset when the knees reconnect or the pass reaches a stable pin.



</section>

<section id="progress-markers" class="content-section">

## Progress Markers
**Beginner Level**:
- Names the supports keeping a partner's arm safe when the roll is paused
- Controls the elbow rather than the wrist when drilling armbar entries
- Reconnects the elbow to the ribs when caught instead of pulling the arm out
- Recognizes when control is lost and resets rather than continuing


**Intermediate Level**:
- Builds a barrier before advancing a kimura or armbar against light resistance
- Isolates one leg to pass rather than fighting both knees at once
- Explains both the attacking and the defensive side of the same exchange
- Releases an isolation that has failed without surrendering position


**Advanced Level**:
- Maintains the isolation through position changes as the opponent turns and scrambles
- Switches to a second target when the first reconnection route is defended
- Uses isolation for sweeps and passes, not only for submissions
- Keeps base while separating so the opponent cannot reverse the reach


**Expert Level**:
- Diagnoses why a partner's isolation fails from one look at the proximal joint
- Times isolation to the opponent's own commitment instead of manufacturing a target
- Trades an isolation for a better position deliberately, including releasing a finish
- Teaches the exchange from both roles using examples across guard, pins and leg entanglements




</section>

<section id="related" class="content-section">

## Related

### Related Principles
- **[[Connection Principles]]** (Prerequisite): Isolation is the deliberate removal of the opponent's connections, so you must be able to read which connections exist before you can strip any of them.
- **[[Elbow-Knee Connection]]** (Complementary): The elbow-knee connection is the defender's primary re-support; the attacker's isolation and the defender's reconnection are the same exchange read from opposite sides.
- **[[Control Point Hierarchy]]** (Complementary): The hierarchy tells you which control point is worth taking; isolation is the mechanism that keeps that point once you have it.
- **[[Levers]]** (Complementary): A limb only becomes a usable lever after it is separated from its supports, so isolation supplies the conditions that leverage then exploits.
- **[[Hyperextension]]** (Extension): Hyperextension is the finishing stage isolation makes possible; applied to a still-connected limb it becomes a strength contest instead of a mechanical break.
- **[[Frames]]** (Complementary): Frames are the supports the defender rebuilds, so every successful frame is an isolation undone and every frame destroyed is an isolation begun.
- **[[Inside Position]]** (Complementary): Inside position decides who can build barriers, which in practice decides which player gets to choose the limb that will be isolated.


### Related Content
- [[Submissions/Armbar|Armbar]] (Submission) - Requires the elbow separated from the ribs and the shoulder denied rotation before the lever exists.
- [[Submissions/Kimura|Kimura]] (Submission) - The model case: two hands isolate one shoulder while the torso is prevented from turning with it.
- [[Transitions/Kneebar|Kneebar]] (Submission) - Isolates one leg from its partner and from the hips so the knee line can be attacked alone.
- [[Submissions/Americana|Americana]] (Submission) - Pins the arm away from the ribs at the elbow; the finish fails entirely if the elbow reconnects.
- [[Submissions/Arm Triangle|Arm Triangle]] (Submission) - Traps one arm across the neck so the isolated limb becomes part of the strangle structure.
- [[Positions/Kimura Trap|Kimura Trap]] (Position) - A position defined purely by an isolated shoulder, from which attacks and transitions both branch.
- [[Positions/Armbar Control|Armbar Control]] (Position) - The holding position for a fully isolated arm, where barriers matter more than finishing pressure.
- [[Positions/Headquarters Position|Headquarters Position]] (Position) - Leg isolation applied to passing — one knee held between the passer's legs so both cannot track together.
- [[Positions/Crucifix|Crucifix]] (Position) - Both arms isolated by separate structures, producing submissions with minimal pressure.
- [[Transitions/Arm Drag|Arm Drag]] (Transition) - Removes a posting arm from its support, converting a defensive limb into an entry to the back.
- [[Principles/Elbow-Knee Connection|Elbow-Knee Connection]] (Principle) - The defender's reconnection standard; isolating a limb means breaking exactly this connection.
- [[Principles/Levers|Levers]] (Principle) - Supplies the mechanics that an isolated limb makes available.
- [[Systems/Danaher Armbar System|Danaher Armbar System]] (System) - A full system built on isolating the arm and denying reconnection before any finishing force is applied.
